summary: Traffic-engineering link attributes were first used with RSVP-TE, but newer applications like Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates also use them. The existing advertisements can't carry application-specific values or show which applications use them. This document defines OSPF advertisements that can. It obsoletes RFC 8920.

eli5.summary: One road sign used to serve every vehicle type. This lets the sign show separate notes for bikes and trucks, and say who each note is for.

questions: what is ospf application specific link attributes
what is the ospf asla sub-tlv type
subtitle: How OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 carry link attributes per application, so RSVP-TE, SR Policy and LFA stop sharing one ambiguous set.

tldr.problem: OSPF link attributes were defined for RSVP-TE, but SR Policy and Loop-Free Alternates use them too. An advertisement for one application could make a router think RSVP-TE was enabled on a link, and each application could not have its own value.
tldr.mechanism: An Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV, placed in the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV or OSPFv3 Router-Link TLV, carries application bit masks followed by the link attribute sub-TLVs those applications use.
tldr.outcome: Each application can have its own attribute values, and new applications can be added without changing the format. RFC 9492 obsoletes RFC 8920 and clarifies zero-length bit masks.

today: RFC 9492 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023. It obsoletes RFC 8920 and has not itself been obsoleted. The matching IS-IS specification is RFC 9479.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Problem
sections.content:
OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) advertise traffic-engineering link attributes through RFC 3630 and RFC 5329, extended by RFC 4203, RFC 7308 and RFC 7471. They were built for MPLS traffic engineering with RSVP, called RSVP-TE (RFC 3209).

Newer applications such as SR Policy (RFC 9256) and Loop-Free Alternates (RFC 5286) use many of the same attributes. If RSVP-TE is enabled on only some links, an attribute advertised for another application on a link can make an RSVP-TE head end assume RSVP-TE is enabled there. Its path setup then fails. Also, the old advertisements cannot hold different values of one attribute for different applications on the same link.

The RFC sets the requirements: indicate which applications use an advertisement, allow application-specific values, allow new applications without format changes, and avoid duplicating link and attribute pairs when a value can be shared.
sections.eli5: Imagine one notice board that both bus drivers and cooks read. A note for the cooks confuses the drivers. This RFC adds a label saying who each note is for.

sections.title: Where the Attributes Live
sections.content:
The existing RSVP-TE attributes travel in the OSPFv2 TE Opaque LSA (RFC 3630) and the OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE-LSA (RFC 5329). For other applications, this RFC uses the Extended Link Opaque LSA (RFC 7684) in OSPFv2 and the E-Router-LSA (RFC 8362) in OSPFv3, which are generic containers for extended link attributes.

The RFC lists the benefits. Advertising there does not make the link part of the RSVP-TE topology. The TE LSAs stay opaque to OSPF, which only transports them. RSVP-TE attributes are clearly separate from those used by other applications. The one disadvantage is that, in rare cases, the same attribute is advertised in both places.

The attribute formats are kept unchanged, but they get new codepoints in the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV Sub-TLVs registry and the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry. TE attributes for RSVP-TE and GMPLS continue to use the TE LSAs.
sections.eli5: RSVP-TE keeps its own old notice board. Everyone else gets a new, general-purpose board, and the notes have the same wording as before.

sections.title: The ASLA Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The ASLA sub-TLV is an optional sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV and the OSPFv3 Router-Link TLV. Its type is 10 in OSPFv2 and 11 in OSPFv3. It holds an SABM Length, a UDABM Length, a reserved field, the two bit masks and the link attribute sub-TLVs.

The SABM (Standard Application Identifier Bit Mask) names standard applications, using bits from the "Link Attribute Application Identifiers" registry in RFC 9479: bit 0 (R-bit) for RSVP-TE, bit 1 (S-bit) for SR Policy and bit 2 (F-bit) for LFA. The UDABM names user-defined applications, which are outside the scope of standardization and not managed by IANA. Each length MUST be 0, 4 or 8 octets, otherwise the sub-TLV MUST be ignored.

The same rules as in IS-IS apply to bits: undefined bits that are sent MUST be 0 and ignored on receipt, bits not sent are treated as 0, and unsupported bits MUST be ignored. The bit masks apply to all attributes in the sub-TLV, so the attribute formats themselves stay unchanged.
sections.eli5: It is a box with a row of switches on top, one per kind of user, and the messages for those users inside.

sections.title: Rules for Using the Values
sections.content:
Several ASLA sub-TLVs can sit in one parent TLV, either because applications control different attributes or because they need different values of the same one. If the same attribute appears in more than one ASLA sub-TLV that lists the application, the application SHOULD use the first and ignore later ones.

Attributes may be sent with zero-length bit masks, meaning any application. Such an advertisement MUST be used when no advertisement with a non-zero mask and a matching bit is present, and MUST NOT be used otherwise. If a new application is introduced and that is not wanted, existing advertisements MUST be readvertised with an explicit set of applications first.

The attributes that MUST use the ASLA sub-TLV when advertised in these TLVs are SRLG, the extended delay, loss and bandwidth metrics from RFC 7471, Administrative Group, Extended Administrative Group and TE Metric. Documents defining new attributes MUST say whether they are application specific.
sections.eli5: If two notes for the same job disagree, read the first one. A note with no "for" line is the fallback when no more specific note fits.

sections.title: Reused Attributes and Codepoints
sections.content:
Each attribute keeps its original format. The SRLG uses the sub-TLV format from RFC 4203, and the extended metrics use the formats from RFC 7471. The TE Metric is type 22 in both protocols.

Three attributes are application independent and MUST NOT appear in the ASLA sub-TLV: maximum link bandwidth (type 23 in both), the Local Interface IPv6 Address (OSPFv3 type 24) and the Remote Interface IPv6 Address (OSPFv3 type 25). They MAY be sent as sub-TLVs of the Extended Link TLV or Router-Link TLV directly. Maximum reservable bandwidth and unreserved bandwidth are not allowed in the ASLA sub-TLV either and MUST stay in the TE LSAs.

The extended performance metrics could in principle be measured per application, but in practice they may be more useful as one value for all traffic on the link. In that case they can be tied to all applications, by listing them or by using a zero-length mask.
sections.eli5: Things that are the same for everybody, like how long the road is, go in the open, not in a note for one group.

sections.title: Enablement and Migration
sections.content:
Whether attributes imply that an application is enabled on a link depends on the application. For RSVP-TE in OSPF, the advertisement of application-specific attributes has no implication of RSVP-TE being enabled; that comes only from the TE Opaque LSA or Intra-Area-TE-LSA. SR Policy is implicitly enabled on all links in the SR-enabled topology, and LFA enablement is local configuration. Future applications MUST define this relationship.

RSVP-TE, and SR Policy or LFA where RSVP-TE is absent or fully congruent, may keep using the RSVP-TE LSA advertisements. New applications MUST NOT use them. While any legacy router has one of these standard applications enabled, all routers MUST use only legacy advertisements and MUST NOT send ASLAs for them. After upgrading, the steps are: send ASLAs alongside legacy ones, enable use of the ASLAs everywhere, and keep legacy advertisements if needed for RSVP-TE. Only then can values differ per application on a link.

It is RECOMMENDED to keep advertising all link attributes for RSVP-TE in the TE LSAs for backwards compatibility.
sections.eli5: Keep posting on the old board until everyone can read the new one. Then move the new stuff across and keep the old board only for the group that still needs it.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 8920
sections.content:
Existing OSPF security mechanisms apply. Where attackers might reach the routing domain, stronger authentication such as that in RFC 5709, RFC 7474, RFC 4552 or RFC 7166 SHOULD be used. Implementations must handle malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs safely. Receipt SHOULD be counted or logged, with logging rate-limited to avoid a denial-of-service attack on the control plane.

Tampering with these advertisements can affect applications such as TE, but because each advertisement is limited to specific applications, so is the impact.

This document replaces RFC 8920. The LSR working group found confusion about advertisements with zero-length masks, because the old text said "permitted", which sounded optional. The replacement text states when they MUST and MUST NOT be used, and a deployment subsection on zero-length masks was added to match RFC 9479.
sections.eli5: Routers should check who is sending notes and not trust garbled ones. A fake note can only upset the group it is aimed at.

fields.name: SABM Length
fields.desc: Standard bit mask length in octets: 0, 4 or 8.

fields.name: UDABM Length
fields.desc: User-defined bit mask length in octets: 0, 4 or 8.
